questions.explanation: A was a common wrong answer, and the cause was not separating base quantities from base units. The ampere is the SI base unit of electric current; the base quantity is current itself, D. The coulomb is a unit too, and charge is not a base quantity because the coulomb is defined as A s. Before choosing, ask of each option: is this the thing being measured, or the unit I measure it in?

The area has an uncertainty of 1.0%, but the volume is built from the side length, so go area → side → volume. Area = L<sup>2</sup>, so the side has half the percentage uncertainty: 1.0 / 2 = 0.5%. Volume = L<sup>3</sup>, so multiply by 3: 3 × 0.5 = 1.5%, which is B. Option C, 3.0%, was the common wrong answer: it multiplies the area's 1.0% by 3 instead of the side's 0.5%. A and D came from treating the area's percentage uncertainty as though it belonged to the side, then converting to volume the wrong way. Name the quantity each percentage belongs to before you multiply.

All four options were popular, and A was the commonest wrong answer. A confuses velocity with speed. With no air resistance, a ball that comes back down to the height it left from has the same speed it left with, but velocity is a vector and its direction has changed, so the velocities are not the same. The horizontal component of acceleration is zero throughout, which is constant: B. C and D mix up velocity and acceleration at the highest point. There the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is not, and the acceleration is still g downwards, so the vertical component of acceleration is not zero either.

The vertical speed at the ground is v<sub>y</sub> = gt = 9.81 × 3.0 = 29.4 m s<sup>−1</sup>. The horizontal speed stays at 10.0 m s<sup>−1</sup>. The two components are at right angles, so the speed is √(10.0<sup>2</sup> + 29.4<sup>2</sup>) = 31 m s<sup>−1</sup>, C. D, 39 m s<sup>−1</sup>, was the commonest wrong answer: 10.0 + 29.4 adds the magnitudes of the components instead of finding the resultant. A, 10 m s<sup>−1</sup>, is the horizontal component on its own, mistaken for the final velocity. Components at right angles never add as plain numbers.

Many candidates chose A. The contact force on the book from the table is equal and opposite to W because the book is in equilibrium, and that is exactly why it is not W's third-law partner: both forces act on the same object, the book. A third-law pair acts on two different objects and is the same type of force. W is the Earth's gravitational pull on the book, so its partner is the book's gravitational pull on the Earth: D. Ask two questions of any candidate pair: same type of force, and different objects?

All the distractors were popular, and few candidates recognised a conservation of momentum problem. Momentum is a vector and the two velocities are at right angles, so the total initial momentum has magnitude 0.16 × √(5.5<sup>2</sup> + 4.2<sup>2</sup>) = 0.16 × 6.9 kg m s<sup>−1</sup>. Q stops, so P carries all of it, and the equal masses cancel: v = 6.9 m s<sup>−1</sup>, C. Many chose D, 9.7 m s<sup>−1</sup>, which is 5.5 + 4.2, adding the magnitudes. Some chose A, 1.3 m s<sup>−1</sup>, the difference of the two. Neither works because the velocities are perpendicular.

All four options were popular, which suggests the definition of the torque of a couple was not secure. A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide. Its torque is the magnitude of one of the forces multiplied by the perpendicular distance between their lines of action. Here that is F × y: C. The length x of the beam is not the perpendicular separation, and 2F would count both forces. Learn the definition in words, then pick out F and y on the diagram.

Some candidates solved the moments correctly and chose B. Many chose C, assuming F<sub>1</sub> and F<sub>2</sub> were equal and ignoring F<sub>3</sub>. The simplest route is to take moments about the weight's line, the centre of gravity, 5.0 cm from the left end, so that W drops out. F<sub>1</sub> (up) is 3.0 cm to the left, F<sub>2</sub> (up) is 3.0 cm to the right and F<sub>3</sub> (down) is 2.0 cm to the right. Clockwise equals anticlockwise: 3.0F<sub>2</sub> = 3.0F<sub>1</sub> + 2.0F<sub>3</sub>. With F<sub>3</sub> = 3F<sub>2</sub>/4 that gives 3.0F<sub>2</sub> = 3.0F<sub>1</sub> + 1.5F<sub>2</sub>, so F<sub>1</sub>/F<sub>2</sub> = ½, B. C is only right if F<sub>3</sub> does nothing.

Many candidates equated the loss in gravitational potential energy to the kinetic energy at the ground, per unit mass: ½v<sup>2</sup> = gh, so v<sup>2</sup> = 2gh. For X, v<sup>2</sup> = 2 × 9.81 × h. For Y, v<sup>2</sup> = 2 × 1.6 × 2h. The ratio of the squares is 9.81 / 3.2 = 3.07, so the ratio of the speeds is √3.07 = 1.75, which is 1.8, B. Many chose D, 3.1, the ratio of the potential energies. That is the ratio of v<sup>2</sup>, and you were asked for v.

Many candidates correctly chose D: the Young modulus is a property of the material, so it does not change as the force changes. The commonest wrong answer was A. The volume of the wire is constant, and the wire gets longer, so its cross-sectional area must get smaller. Because the area falls, stress (F / A) rises, and the strain rises too, so B and C change as well. Read the conditions the question sets: constant volume was the clue.

All the options were popular and the distractors were chosen about equally, so the series and parallel rules were not secure. For identical springs of constant k, springs in parallel add: k<sub>eff</sub> = 2k. Springs in series share the load and the effective constant falls: for two, k/2. Arrangement C is two columns side by side, each a series pair: each column has k/2, and the two columns in parallel give k/2 + k/2 = k, the same as a single spring. A is a series pair (k/2), B a parallel pair (2k), and D is a parallel pair in series with one spring (2k/3). Build up from the inside: do the series parts first, then the parallel.

Few candidates realised that a train moving at constant velocity gives a constant frequency at the student, and most chose D, which shows the Doppler effect is not well understood. In f<sub>o</sub> = f<sub>s</sub>v / (v − v<sub>s</sub>), nothing on the right changes while the train approaches at constant speed, so the student hears one steady note: C. A frequency that keeps rising (D) would need the train to be speeding up. The frequency only changes if the relative speed changes.

A and C were often selected, so the wavelength ranges of the main regions of the spectrum were not secure. 0.1 nm is 1 × 10<sup>−10</sup> m, which is in the X-ray region: D. Infrared (A) has wavelengths thousands of times longer, and visible light (C) is of the order of 10<sup>−7</sup> m. When you can, convert to metres first and compare the powers of ten.

Very few candidates used both relationships. The power on a surface is intensity × area, and the intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. Tripling the amplitude multiplies the intensity by 3<sup>2</sup> = 9, and tripling the area multiplies it by 3 again: 9 × 3 = 27, so 27P, D. B and C were common: B applies the area alone (3P) and C the amplitude alone (9P). Candidates had one relationship but not the other.

The distractors were chosen evenly, so many candidates did not know how to start. Five nodes with a node at each end make four loops, so the length is L = 4 × λ/2 = 2λ. Increasing the frequency slowly, the next stationary wave has six nodes, five loops: L = 5 × λ′/2, so λ′ = 2L/5 = 0.8λ. Frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength, so f′ = f / 0.8 = 1.25f: A. Count loops, not nodes, when you relate the length to the wavelength.

Most candidates recalled that the wavelength does not change in diffraction, so they chose A or B. The deciding point is the gap. In the diagram it is about the same size as the wavelength, which is where the waves spread out most, and widening it makes the spreading gradually smaller, so the angle θ decreases: A.

All three distractors were equally popular, so the equation was not being applied well. The fringe spacing is x = λD / a, so to halve it you can double the slit separation a or halve the distance D to the screen, but not both. Doubling a with D unchanged is A. B doubles D, which doubles the spacing to 10 cm. C halves a and doubles D, a factor of 4 (20 cm). D doubles a and halves D, a factor of 1/4 (1.25 cm). Change one thing at a time and work out the factor.

R = ρL/A. With the length and resistivity fixed, R is inversely proportional to A: double the area and the resistance halves. That is graph B, a curve that falls steeply at small A and levels off without reaching the axis. The report found many candidates saw that R falls as A rises but couldn't recall the shape of an inverse graph. That describes the straight falling line, A. A straight line would reach R = 0 at a finite area, which no wire can do. For any inverse relationship, look for the curve.

The responses were spread across the wrong options, and the question needs careful analysis of the circuit. The simplest approach is to find the p.d. across, or the current in, each resistor. B and C are in parallel: 1/R = 1/2.0 + 1/1.0, so R = 0.67 Ω. The total resistance is 0.33 + 0.67 + 3.0 = 4.0 Ω, so the current from the cell is 12 / 4.0 = 3.0 A. A and D carry all of it: P = I<sup>2</sup>R = 3.0 W for A and 27 W for D. The parallel pair has 3.0 × 0.67 = 2.0 V across it, so P = V<sup>2</sup>/R gives 2.0 W for B and 4.0 W for C. B dissipates the least.

Most candidates chose A. Kirchhoff's second law is about potential differences round a loop: the e.m.f. equals the sum of the p.d.s. In A, 6.0 V + 3.0 V across the two series resistors adds up to the 9.0 V of the cell. B was chosen by those who confused the sum of p.d.s in series with parallel: in parallel each resistor would have the full 9.0 V, not 4.5 V each. D was chosen by those who confused the two laws: it shows currents at a junction, which is Kirchhoff's first law.

Some candidates compared the resistances in the two branches, found the p.d. at each mid-point, and chose B. The left branch is 24.0 + 6.0 = 30.0 Ω, so its current is 15.0 / 30.0 = 0.50 A and the lower 6.0 Ω has 3.0 V across it. The right branch is 6.0 + 9.0 = 15.0 Ω, so its current is 1.0 A and the lower 9.0 Ω has 9.0 V across it. Measured from the same bottom wire, the voltmeter reads the difference: 9.0 − 3.0 = 6.0 V. A, 3.0 V, is the p.d. across the 6.0 Ω resistor, and C, 9.0 V, is the p.d. across the 9.0 Ω resistor. Each is one side's potential, not the difference.

Some candidates correctly identified the changes in the readings. When the light intensity increases, the resistance of the LDR falls, so the total resistance falls and the current rises: the ammeter reading increases. The voltmeter is across the fixed resistor, so its p.d. is IR with R fixed, and it increases too: D. B was chosen perhaps by those who looked at the p.d. across the LDR, which does fall. C would need the current to fall and rise at the same time, which would require the resistance of the LDR to both increase and decrease.
